storySections.caption: The botany laboratory in 1998. Dissecting hibiscus flowers while deciding what life outside Madurai might look like.

storySections.heading: Now — The Blue Notebook
storySections.body:
Three months ago, Anjali called me.

Anjali had lived three houses down from Kavitha during our school days. Her parents were finally selling the ancestral family house on Bishop Wallers Avenue—a beautiful, crumbling Art Deco bungalow with red-tiled roofs that was being razed to make way for eight luxury apartments with stilt parking. Anjali had spent a fortnight clearing out the attic, where two generations of trunks had accumulated layers of cobwebs and silverfish.

'Meera,' she said over the phone, her voice crackling with the dust of old paper. 'I found a carton from our college study groups. There are three cartons of old class notes, old cassette tapes, and a couple of diaries. Some of them are yours, some are Kavitha's. Do you want me to throw them out or do you want to look?'

I drove to Bishop Wallers Avenue that evening before the traffic on TTK Road thickened.

The house smelled of damp plaster, naphthalene balls, and that particular melancholy scent of empty cupboards. In the center of the hall sat six cardboard boxes taped with brown packing tape. Anjali made me instant coffee in a chipped stainless-steel tumbler and pointed to the box marked Notes / Misc 1999–2004.

I sat on a plastic stool among the stripped walls and began lifting out the past.

There were old record sheets for organic chemistry, loose-leaf papers covered in my frantic, illegible scrawl, printed movie tickets from the old Devi Paradise cinema, and a cassette tape of A.R. Rahman's Alaipayuthey with the plastic case cracked down the center. And near the bottom, wedged between a textbook on fluid dynamics and an empty fountain pen box, lay a small blue hardbound notebook with cloth-bound corners.

It was Kavitha's journal from 1999.

I recognized the handwriting instantly—her lettering was tiny, upright, and so uniform it resembled printing. She never used ballpoint pens; she wrote exclusively with a black Camlin fountain pen that her uncle had brought her from Bombay.

I should have closed it. A private diary is a room you have no right to enter unless you have been invited across the threshold, and nobody had invited me into Kavitha's life for almost two decades. But guilt has its own voyeurism. I sat on that red plastic stool in a dying house and turned the pages until I found the date: September 14, 1999.

It was the week of her eighteenth birthday.

There were four lines on the ruled page, written in that precise, unhurried black ink:

Meera called from the campus booth at 4 PM to say she had a rehearsal for the youth festival and would be two hours late. It is now 9:30. Amma has put the payasam in the fridge. I told Appa to go to sleep. I think I am going to stop leaving the gate unlatched.

That was all.

No exclamation marks. No tears smeared across the paper. No furious paragraphs dissecting my selfishness or mourning the death of our childhood. Just a quiet, surgical statement of fact: I think I am going to stop leaving the gate unlatched.

I stared at those four lines until the letters blurred into blue-black smears. I sat there in the silence of Anjali's dusty hall, the cold steel tumbler resting against my kneecap, and felt the specific, sickening lurch of an elevator whose cable has snapped under your feet.
storySections.alt: An open botanical field notebook with pressed flower specimens and detailed sketches beside a fountain pen
storySections.caption: The blue ruled notebook from 2004. Twelve dried bougainvillea petals pressed between pages of handwritten dreams.

storySections.chapterTitle: 2011 — The Woodlands Drive-in That Never Happened
storySections.heading: 2011 — The Woodlands Drive-in That Never Happened
storySections.body:
By 2011, Woodlands Drive-in was already living on borrowed time—the municipal leases were expiring, the lawyers were filing stays in the High Court, and the sprawling compound off Cathedral Road with its ancient raintrees, its gravel bays, and its servers balancing steel trays on half-rolled-down car windows had the melancholy glamour of an era about to be demolished for a public park.

I was thirty-five. I was a vice-president at an agency in T. Nagar. I drove a silver Honda City with tinted glass, had two phones that chimed with different polyphonic rings, and spoke in the breathless, compressed shorthand of people who believe that being constantly interrupted is proof of their social indispensability.

Kavitha was back in Chennai for six weeks. Her mother had suffered a minor paralytic stroke—nothing fatal, but enough to leave her left hand curled like a dry leaf and her speech slurred at the vowels. Kavitha had taken unpaid leave from her laboratory in Dundee, flown down on twenty-four hours' notice, and spent three weeks sleeping on a wooden bench in the verandah of the Chromepet house while nurses came and went with saline drips.

She had called me twice. Both times my assistant had taken a message while I was in client meetings. When I finally called back from my car on a Thursday evening, she asked if we could meet.

'Not your office, Meera,' she had said. Her voice over the phone sounded dry, thin, stripped of all ambient resonance by the international roaming connection. 'Just one hour. Woodlands. Five o'clock on Saturday? Before my mother's evening physiotherapist arrives.'

'Done,' I said instantly. 'Woodlands. Five sharp. We'll get the filter coffee and the masala vadai like we used to. Kavi, I've missed you so much. There is so much I need to tell you about the London account.'

'Five o'clock,' she repeated.

On Saturday at four-thirty, I was in my car on the Gemini flyover when the senior brand director for our largest telecom client called. The client was in town from Singapore. He had three hours before his flight back to Changi. He wanted to review the revised storyboard for the Diwali campaign over drinks at the Park Hotel, which was precisely four hundred yards from Woodlands Drive-in.

I looked at my watch. 4:38 PM.

If I went to Woodlands, I would see Kavitha for forty-five minutes, rush away smelling of onion sambar, arrive late to the Park Hotel, and look like someone who had priorities outside the agency. If I postponed Kavitha, she was in town for another three weeks. We could meet on Tuesday. Or next Saturday. Kavitha was my best friend; Kavitha would understand. Clients did not understand; clients had procurement committees.

I dialed her mobile. The phone rang five times.

'Kavi? Listen, you won't believe the catastrophe here. The Singapore team landed unexpectedly. It's the regional head—if I don't show face, they'll pull the entire fourth-quarter retainer. Can we do Tuesday instead? Same time, Woodlands? I promise I'll make it up to you.'

There was a silence on the line. Through the receiver, I could hear the background sounds of Woodlands: the crunch of tires on gravel, the clatter of heavy ceramic cups against tin trays, the low hum of Tamil radio playing from an Ambassador parked nearby.

She was already there.

She had arrived at twenty to five. She had taken an auto from Chromepet—a forty-minute journey in the heat of a May afternoon—so she wouldn't be late.

'Are you already there?' I asked, my voice dropping an octave.

'I've ordered the cold coffee,' she said. Her voice was perfectly even. It had that terrible, polite clarity that strangers use when returning an incorrect umbrella. 'It's fine, Meera. Go to your meeting.'

'Kavi, don't be like that! I'll come for twenty minutes—'

'No,' she said. Not loudly. Just with the absolute finality of a lock sliding into a brass groove. 'Don't come for twenty minutes. Go to your meeting.'

She hung up.

I sat in the air-conditioned cabin of my Honda City on the ramp of the Gemini flyover, with the engine idling and the indicators blinking. For twelve seconds, I had my hand on the steering wheel, ready to take the left turn down toward Cathedral Road. I could park beside the raintree. I could walk across the gravel. I could sit in the wicker chair opposite her, apologize without defending myself, and drink the cold coffee.

Then the client's assistant texted: Mr. Tan is in the lobby lounge. Table 4.

I turned right toward the Park Hotel.

I told myself I would send a bouquet of lilies to Chromepet on Monday. I told myself I would take her to the Taj for dinner next weekend. I told myself that adult life was full of these minor collisions between friendship and survival, and that people who loved you understood that survival had to come first.

I sent the lilies. The delivery service returned a receipt signed by a cousin.

On Tuesday, when I called, her phone switched straight to voicemail. On Friday, when I sent a message, the double tick stayed grey. When she flew back to Scotland ten days later, she did not call to say goodbye.

I told my husband that night: 'Kavitha has become very difficult lately. You try your best to maintain these old bonds, but people change when they go abroad. They expect you to drop everything at their convenience.'

He nodded without looking up from his laptop. It was an agreeable, comforting lie. We ate our dinner. The world continued.

storySections.chapterTitle: Then — The Autumn We Turned Eighteen
storySections.heading: Then — The Autumn We Turned Eighteen
storySections.body:
I remember that September evening with terrifying clarity now, stripped of all the convenient fog with which I had insulated my memory.

We had both entered college that July. I had gained admission to Stella Maris for English Literature—a boisterous, sun-drenched world of theater societies, debate competitions, coffee sessions at the canteen, and boys from Loyola waiting at the bus stop with acoustic guitars. I took to it like a fish released into open water. I joined the drama club; I auditioned for three plays; I began wearing silver jhumkas that swung against my shoulders and smoking the occasional Classic Mild behind the basketball courts with girls who quoted Sylvia Plath and talked about feminism with breathless authority.

Kavitha had enrolled at a quiet women's college in Kilpauk to study Botany. Her campus was smaller, stricter, surrounded by high whitewashed walls and tall gulmohar trees. She commuted on the suburban train every morning with a tiffin box in her bag, returned home by four, and spent her evenings drawing cross-sections of plant stems with a 2B pencil.

Whenever she called our landline, my mother would hand me the receiver while I was halfway out the door to an audition or a friend's birthday party.

'Kavitha,' I would say, tucking the black receiver between my ear and collarbone while hunting for my dupatta. 'Listen, I have to run—the street play team is meeting at the beach. Can I call you back at ten?'

'Sure,' she would say. Her voice was always even. 'Don't worry.'

I never called back at ten. At ten I would be sitting at an Irani tea stall on Besant Nagar beach eating bun butter jam and talking about Virginia Woolf with people whose names I would completely forget by my third year.

For her eighteenth birthday—September 14—she had invited six people to her house on Fourth Main Road. Her mother, who made the best vadai in the neighborhood, had spent the entire morning frying savouries and preparing semiya payasam with roasted cashews and golden raisins.

I had promised to be there at five. 'Five sharp,' I had said on Sunday evening. 'I'll bring the cake from Bosotto Brothers. Don't buy one.'

At three that afternoon, the drama club convener announced an emergency rehearsal for the inter-collegiate festival in Bangalore. It was a chaotic, exhilarating meeting in the auditorium. Everyone was arguing about lighting and costume fabric. I looked at the wall clock at four, ran out to the coin-box phone outside the library, and dropped a one-rupee coin into the slot.

'Kavitha? Listen, disaster. Sister Philomena called an extra rehearsal. I'm stuck here till six. Is it okay if I come by seven? Keep my payasam aside!'

'We haven't cut the cake,' she said quietly.

'Don't wait for me to cut the cake! Cut it with your cousins, I'll be there soon!'

The rehearsal ran past seven. Then someone suggested going to the printer on Mount Road to pick up the festival posters. Then the auto broke down near Gemini Flyover. By the time I actually bought a rather battered pineapple pastry from an ordinary bakery and hailed another rickshaw to Fourth Main Road, it was twenty minutes past nine.

The gate was closed.

Not locked with the heavy brass padlock, but latched firmly from the inside with the iron bolt. The veranda light was off.

I opened the latch, my sandals crunching loudly on the red gravel. I knocked on the front door, panting, rehearsing my charming, breathless apology.

Kavitha's mother opened the door. She was wearing her old night saree—the faded green cotton one with the border unravelled at the hem. She didn't look angry; she looked exhausted, the way women look when they have spent ten hours standing over a hot stove for a celebration that never caught fire.

'Aunty,' I stammered, holding up the bakery box like an offering. 'I am so, so sorry. The traffic at Gemini—'

'Kavitha has gone to sleep, Meera,' she said softly. She didn't open the door wider. She didn't invite me in.

'Can I just see her for two minutes? Just to give her the cake?'

'She's tired. She has an early practical exam tomorrow.' Her mother looked down at the white cardboard box in my hands. 'Leave it on the veranda table if you want. Goodnight, Meera.'

She closed the wooden door. The bolt slid into place with a sharp, dry snap.

I stood on that porch in the dark for a long time. The crickets were shrill in the hibiscus bushes. I felt a sudden, cold prickle of humiliation—not guilt, but humiliation, because I had been dismissed like a stranger at the door of a house where I had spent half my childhood afternoons eating mangoes on the kitchen floor.

She'll call me tomorrow, I told myself as I walked out the gate. Once she's slept it off, she'll call.

She did not call the next day. Nor the day after that.

A week later, I called her house. Her father answered, said she was at the library, and hung up. When we finally ran into each other outside the post office in October, she was polite. She asked about my plays. She smiled when I made a joke about our old geography teacher. But when I suggested going to the juice shop near the bus terminus for watermelon juice—our old ritual whenever either of us had ten rupees—she looked at her watch and said she had to catch the 4:15 bus.

There was no shouting. There was no confrontation. There was simply an invisible pane of thick, laminated glass dropped between us. I could see her through it; she could see me. But when I knocked, my knuckles made no sound.

storySections.heading: The Biology of Fatigue
storySections.body:
In the week after I found the blue notebook in the cleared-out flat on Bishop Wallers Avenue, I did not call the number in Edinburgh that was penciled on the back cover.

I wanted to. I had the phone in my hand three times—once at midnight while sitting in the dark of my kitchen, once at six in the morning while the crows were waking in the neem trees outside our terrace, and once from the parking lot of my office in Alwarpet. Each time, my thumb hovered over the green button, and each time, something hard and cold seized my throat.

What would I say?

Hello, Kavitha? It's Meera. I found your notebook. I read what you wrote in 1999 about the raintree. I'm sorry about 2011. I'm sorry about 2007. I'm sorry that I was busy when your mother had a stroke.

It sounded grotesque. It sounded like an audit of debts by someone who only remembered she owed money when she found the ledger in the trash.

Instead, on Thursday morning, I drove out to Taramani—to the coastal research laboratory where Kavitha had worked before she left India for good.

It was still there, tucked behind the railway embankment where the MRTS trains rattle on elevated concrete piers. The building had acquired the grey, rain-streaked patina of all government institutions in South India: peeling lime wash, water coolers dripping into plastic buckets, and long corridors smelling of phenyl and formaldehyde.

I asked the security guard for Dr. Rangan's old department. He directed me to the second floor, to a room labeled Plant Stress Physiology.

The room was occupied by an elderly man in a faded safari suit who was examining pressed herbarium sheets under a magnifying glass. His nameplate said Dr. K. Swaminathan, Emeritus Scientist.

'Kavitha?' he said when I introduced myself as an old college friend. His spectacles had thick tortoiseshell frames, and his eyes swam behind them like small fish in round bowls. 'Dr. Kavitha Rangan? She hasn't been in this department since 2014. She's at the Royal Botanic Garden now. Very distinguished career. We still cite her monograph on mangrove osmoregulation.'

'I know,' I said. 'I just... I was passing by.'

He looked at me over the rims of his glasses. Older teachers have an instinct for the unstated motives of adults who visit them unannounced; they have seen generations of students return carrying various forms of belated regret.

'You were at Presidency?' he asked.

'Yes. With her.'

He nodded slowly. He set down his herbarium sheet, took off his spectacles, and wiped them with the tail of his safari shirt.

'She worked very hard in this room,' he said. 'Too hard, perhaps. In those years, after her father passed away, she was supporting her mother and two younger brothers on an eighty-percent research stipend. She used to walk from the railway station to save eight rupees of bus fare every single day, rain or shine. In July, her canvas slippers would be soaked through. She would take them off at the door, put on the lab sandals, and work until nine at night.'

A cold knot tightened in my chest. 'I didn't know about the bus fare.'

The old man looked at me, not unkindly, but with the quiet neutrality of a scientist observing an irreversible chemical reaction.

'She wouldn't have told you,' he said. 'Kavitha was a girl of immense self-respect. If someone was interested, she answered. If they were not, she did not volunteer her difficulties. People who carry heavy loads alone develop that posture. They stop expecting others to notice the weight.'

He picked up his magnifying glass again.

'She waited for people, you know,' he added, almost as an afterthought, his eyes already returning to the veining of a dried leaf. 'When she was here, before she went to Scotland, she used to keep her Friday evenings open. She would sit on that stone bench by the nursery until six o'clock, waiting to see if anyone from her old circle would come by for tea. Then, around six-fifteen, she would pack her bag and walk to the station alone.'

I didn't say anything. There was nothing to say.

I thanked him and walked down the wide, echoing stairs. In the courtyard outside, beneath the canopy of a massive gulmohar tree, stood the stone bench he had mentioned. It was stained with bird droppings and fallen red petals, cool in the coastal shade.

I sat on the bench.

I sat there for twenty minutes while the suburban trains rumbled overhead on the concrete tracks, shaking the leaves.

I understood, finally, the exact architecture of what I had done. I had not betrayed Kavitha with a dramatic cruelty; I had simply starved her of attention until she withered out of my life. I had accepted her loyalty as a permanent background feature of my world, like the water supply or the electricity, assuming it would always flow when I turned the tap, and never once wondering who was paying the bill.

She had not stopped being my friend because she hated me. She had stopped because she was tired.

Because after fifteen years of being the only one who remembered birthdays, the only one who showed up on time, the only one who asked about the mother, the only one who sat on the stone bench until six-fifteen, she had quietly, decently, without making a scene, decided to put the heavy thing down.

I stood up from the stone bench. I walked to my car. I put the blue notebook on the passenger seat, turned the ignition, and drove back to the city that we had shared when we were young, and which now belonged to each of us separately.

storySections.heading: Now — The Tamil Film
storySections.body:
Last Sunday night, I watched Kandukondain Kandukondain alone on my laptop.

It was the film we were supposed to watch together in the summer of 2000. We had planned it for six months before its release. A.R. Rahman's soundtrack had come out on cassette tape in February, and we had spent hours sitting on her terrace rewinding Kannamoochi Yenada with a pencil, analyzing every flute line, deciding which of the two sisters in the film resembled each of us.

'I'm definitely Sowmya,' she had said, leaning her back against the warm water tank. 'The practical one who worries about the electricity bill.'

'And I'm Meenakshi,' I had declared, shaking my hair loose. 'The romantic one who recites poetry in the rain.'

'Meenakshi gets her heart broken because she doesn't pay attention to reality,' Kavitha had remarked, dryly, not looking up from her botany sketches. 'Don't forget that part.'

When the film finally opened in May at the Devi theater complex, I had tickets for the opening Friday. But my college theater group had just been invited to perform at a youth festival in Trivandrum. I sold our tickets to a neighbor's son, sent Kavitha a postcard from Kerala with a picture of a houseboat, and wrote: Next week, I promise! Devi Paradise 3 PM show!

By next week, I was in Bangalore. By the time I returned, the film had moved to a smaller hall in George Town. By July, it was gone.

I sat on my sofa in Alwarpet at midnight, twenty-four years later, with a glass of warm water, watching the remastered digital print. When the opening credits rolled and the flute melody began, a sudden, violent knot formed in the center of my throat.

It wasn't even a masterpiece. It had all the usual flaws of turn-of-the-millennium commercial cinema—unnecessary comedy tracks, melodramatic violins, actors wearing wigs that didn't quite match their sideburns. But every frame felt like an indictment. I kept looking at the empty space on the sofa next to me, where an eighteen-year-old girl with coconut oil in her hair and a yellow kurta should have been sitting, groaning at the dialogue and passing me a paper cone of salted peanuts.

I paused the video at the scene where Tabu sits on the rain-soaked veranda of their village home, looking at the empty gate.

I opened my laptop browser and searched for her name.

It was absurdly easy to find her. The modern world does not allow anyone to disappear completely.

Dr. Kavitha Rangan, Ph.D. Associate Professor, Department of Plant Molecular Biology, National Centre for Biological Sciences, Bangalore.

There was a photograph on the university faculty page. She was forty-one in the picture. Her hair was cut shorter, just brushing her collarbones, shot through with bold streaks of silver at the temples that she had clearly chosen not to dye. She was wearing a simple handloom cotton saree and rimless glasses. She had the calm, self-possessed gaze of a woman who spends her working hours looking into electron microscopes, measuring the respiration rates of rice leaves under drought conditions.

Below the photograph was an office landline number and an email address.

I stared at that seven-digit Bangalore landline for forty-five minutes while the movie played on mute behind the browser window.

storySections.heading: Then — The Gradual Erasure
storySections.body:
The friendship did not end with a bang; it eroded through a hundred tiny cancellations.

Between the ages of nineteen and twenty-three, I saw Kavitha exactly four times. Each meeting was initiated by me, usually after a sudden surge of nostalgia or guilt triggered by an old photograph or a song on the radio.

'Kavi!' I would say, calling her hostel landline in Bangalore after she had moved there for her Master's degree. 'I'm coming to Bangalore for an interview next weekend! We have to meet. Saturday evening, Brigade Road, okay?'

'I have lab work on Saturday until five,' she would say. 'I can meet you at the coffee house at six.'

'Six is perfect!'

At six on Saturday, I would be stuck in a meeting with a college friend who had just moved to Koramangala. At 6:45, I would call her from a public booth.

'Kavi, traffic on Hosur Road is insane. Can we do 7:30?'

'Meera, the hostel gates close at eight.'

'Then come to my hotel! Stay over!'

'I have a seminar presentation on Monday morning, Meera. All my slides are in the department.'

'Just for an hour?'

'I don't think so. Let's try next time you're in town.'

And the terrible, unforgivable thing was that each time she refused to contort her schedule around my tardiness, a small, ugly voice inside me whispered that she was the difficult one. Look at how inflexible she has become, I would tell my other friends over drinks. She used to be so easygoing. Now she acts like a government clerk. If you're fifteen minutes late, she packs up her books and leaves.

I genuinely believed that. I had convinced myself that my spontaneity was a virtue and her punctuality was a defect. I thought that true friendship meant unconditional forgiveness for bad manners.

The last time I saw her in person was in December of 2007.

We were twenty-six. She was visiting her parents in Chennai for Pongal; I had just returned from two years of working in Mumbai. We met at the Woodlands Drive-in on Cathedral Road—the old one, before they turned it into a botanical park, where you could park under the banyan trees and waiters in white uniforms would bring stainless-steel trays of rava dosa directly to your car window.

She had arrived on an electric scooter. She was sitting at one of the round stone tables under the banyan tree when I arrived twenty minutes late.

She stood up, smiled, and hugged me. It was a warm hug, but it lasted two seconds. It had the measured, diplomatic courtesy of an embassy official greeting a delegate from an unaligned nation.

We ordered filter coffee. We talked about her research on mycorrhizal fungi; we talked about my job at the infrastructure firm. She listened attentively. She laughed when I imitated our old botany teacher. But whenever the conversation drifted toward the past—toward our bicycle rides, the red pencil box, the afternoons on her terrace—she gently steered it back to the present.

'That was a long time ago, Meera,' she said once, stirring two packets of brown sugar into her coffee.

'It doesn't feel that long,' I protested.

She looked at me across the stone table. Her eyes were very clear, very steady behind her spectacles.

'It is long,' she said, without heat. 'We've been other people for ten years now.'

When the waiter brought the bill, she took out a twenty-rupee note, placed it on the saucer, and picked up her scooter keys.

'It was good to see you, Meera. Take care of yourself.'

'Let me take your number in Bangalore,' I said, scrambling to find my phone in my handbag. 'I'm coming there for a conference in March.'

She gave me the number. She did not ask for mine.

storySections.heading: Now — The Call
storySections.body:
Yesterday afternoon, at a quarter past three, I dialed the office landline at the National Centre for Biological Sciences.

I had rehearsed the call for three days. I had written notes on the back of a utility bill: Don't apologize too much. Don't make excuses about college or youth festivals. Just tell her you found the notebook. Tell her you finally understood.

The phone rang four times. The ringtone had that flat, institutional hum of government scientific facilities.

A woman's voice answered on the fifth ring:

'Plant Physiology and Genetics. Dr. Rangan's lab.'

'Hello,' I said, my throat so dry the word cracked in the middle. 'Could I speak to Dr. Kavitha Rangan, please?'

'One moment.'

The receiver was set down on a hard surface. In the background, I could hear the rhythmic clatter of glass test tubes, the low whir of a centrifuge, and someone in the hallway asking about liquid nitrogen delivery. Real work. A real life, constructed brick by brick, experiment by experiment, across twenty-four years of my total absence.

Then the receiver was lifted.

'Kavitha Rangan speaking.'

Her voice was deeper than I remembered, stripped of the high, musical lilt of our adolescence, but underneath the professional cadence, the cadence of Thiruvanmiyur and Harrington Road was still there, as indelible as granite.

'Kavitha,' I said. 'It's Meera.'

A silence followed. Not a long silence—perhaps three seconds. Just long enough for an intelligent person to search through several filing cabinets of memory and locate a folder marked Childhood / Obsolete.

'Meera,' she said. Her tone was completely steady. 'Hello.'

'Hello,' I said. I looked down at the notes on my utility bill. Every word I had written seemed suddenly childish, insulting, an absurd imposition on an adult stranger's working afternoon. 'I... I got your number from the NCBS website. I hope it's not a bad time.'

'I have a doctoral committee meeting in fifteen minutes,' she said, neither warm nor cold. 'Is everything alright? Are your parents well?'

'Yes. Yes, everyone is well. Ma is in Coimbatore with my brother.' I took a breath. 'Kavitha, I was at Anjali's house three months ago. They're selling the property. She found a carton of old things from college. Your blue notebook was in it.'

'Ah,' she said. A brief, quiet sound. 'The one from ninety-nine.'

'Yes.'

'I had wondered where that went. It's mostly notes on angiosperms, isn't it?'

'There was an entry from September fourteenth,' I said. The words came out before I could stop them. 'Your eighteenth birthday.'

The line hummed with static. I could hear someone outside her office door knocking twice.

'Meera,' she said gently.

That single word, spoken in that particular tone, did what no anger could ever have done: it closed the door forever. It was the tone an adult uses with a child who has brought a broken toy to the table long after everyone has finished eating.

'I'm sorry,' I whispered. 'I was late for everything. I was late for ten years.'

There was another pause. When she spoke again, her voice was not unkind, but it was impenetrable.

'Meera, that was a quarter of a century ago. We were children. You don't need to carry an apology around for twenty-five years for being eighteen and foolish.'

'It wasn't just being foolish,' I said, fighting the sudden, humiliating tremor in my voice. 'I didn't pay attention. I thought you would always be there at the postbox.'

'And I wasn't,' she said simply. 'And that's alright. People grow in different directions. That's what plants do, Meera. They grow toward whatever light is available to them.'

Someone knocked on her office door again, louder this time.

'Dr. Rangan?' a male voice called out in the room. 'The committee members from IISc are in the conference room.'

'I'll be right there, Vinod,' she answered away from the receiver. Then she returned to me. 'Meera, I have to go now.'

'Will you... can I send you the notebook?' I asked, grasping at the last thread. 'I have it in my drawer. I can courier it to your lab.'

'Keep it,' she said, with the faintest trace of a smile in her voice. 'Or throw it away. I have three filing cabinets full of data now. I don't need the notes on angiosperms.'

'Kavitha—'

'It was good to hear your voice, Meera. Truly. I hope you are happy.'

The line went dead with a clean, electronic click.

I sat at my desk in Alwarpet with the receiver in my hand. The dial tone began its mechanical drone. Outside the window, the rain tree stood motionless in the midday heat, its branches heavy with dark leaves, growing toward whatever light was available.

title: The Last Bench Promise
description: In 1998, two eleven-year-old boys carved their initials into the last bench of Class 9B and made a pact before a sudden family transfer. Twenty-six years later, an ornate wedding invitation arrives on a phone screen.
excerpt: The last bench of Room 9 had one leg half an inch shorter than the others. It was stabilized by a folded strip of grey cardboard from an old geometry notebook, replaced every term like an offering.
author: Noble John Steeven

storySections.chapterTitle: Scene 1: The Gold Card on the Screen (2024)
storySections.heading: Scene 1: The Gold Card on the Screen (2024)
storySections.body:
The invitation arrived on a Tuesday evening in late October, wedged between a video of a toddler wrestling a golden retriever and an announcement about municipal water rationing in Mayur Vihar.

Dhruv Malhotra was sitting in his 2014 Maruti Swift in the basement parking lot of his apartment complex, the air conditioning blowing lukewarm air through vents that smelled of damp foam. He had turned the engine off three minutes ago, but he had not opened the door. The fifteen minutes between parking the car and stepping into the lift were the only fifteen minutes of the day when nobody required him to approve an invoice, sign a vendor manifest, or arbitrate a dispute between his seven-year-old daughter and nine-year-old son over the television remote.

The WhatsApp notification came from a group called *St. Jude's Batch of '99*.

It was a dead group, mostly. Four times a year, someone's cousin would post an unverified greeting for Diwali or Eid with animated oil lamps, and three people would reply with folded-hand emojis before the thread subsided back into the digital silt. But this message was an image file—a scanned wedding card bordered in heavy embossed maroon and gold foil.

*Mr. & Mrs. Farooq Qureshi request the pleasure of your company at the wedding reception of their son, Sameer, with Dr. Zoya Alvi.*

Dhruv enlarged the image until the pixels broke into yellow squares.

Sameer Qureshi.

A physical sensation hit Dhruv just below the breastbone—not a pain, exactly, but a hollow, suction-like thump, like stepping off a curb in the dark and finding the road six inches lower than your heel anticipated. He was thirty-seven years old. His black hair had developed a dense, salt-and-pepper frost along the jawline that his wife Pallavi said made him look distinguished, though he knew it merely made him look like a man who spent ten hours a day managing cold-chain logistics for imported pharmaceuticals.

He had not spoken to Sameer since the summer of 2001.

Twenty-three years. He had spent six months in 2016, right before his own wedding, trying to find Sameer's contact details. He had messaged three different school seniors on LinkedIn, called an old landline number in Pune that had been reassigned to a veterinary clinic, and even checked the directory of the Maharashtra state engineering council. Nothing. Sameer had simply dropped out of the Delhi registry as cleanly as if he had stepped through a curtain into another country.

Sameer had missed Dhruv's wedding. He had not known about it, of course; Dhruv could not blame a man for failing to attend an event he had never been told was happening. But on that November night in 2016, while standing on a carpeted stage in Pitampura in a rented sherwani that pinched his armpits, shaking hands with three hundred distant relatives whose names he had forgotten by morning, Dhruv had caught himself looking toward the entrance gate every time a new group of cars pulled up.

He tapped the screen. He opened the profile of the person who had posted the card—a boy named Varun Kapoor who had sat two benches ahead of them in eighth standard and now ran an advertising firm in Gurgaon.

*Varun, hi. Dhruv Malhotra here. Do you have Sameer's actual number?*

He sat in the dark car for eight minutes until his phone buzzed.

*Hey Dhruv! Long time man. Yes, here you go: 98230-XXXXX. He's based in Pune now, building bridges or something.*

Dhruv copied the ten digits into his dialer. His thumb hovered over the green button. Then he stopped, backed out, and opened the message screen instead. What did an adult man say to another adult man after twenty-three years of silence without sounding either hysterical or pathetic?

He typed four words:

*Sameer? It's Dhruv. Delhi.*

storySections.heading: Scene 2: Room 9, Class 9B (1998)
storySections.body:
Room 9 had four windows that looked out over the dry, unwatered football field of St. Jude's High School, where the April dust rose in yellow devils whenever the physical education teacher made the ninth standard run laps.

The last bench in the row closest to the wall was their territory.

It was an ancient piece of furniture, constructed from three-inch planks of dark Sheesham wood that had resisted sixty years of pocketknives, compass tips, and leaky inkwells. The right rear leg was half an inch shorter than the other three, giving the bench a sharp, irritating wobble whenever someone leaned on their elbows. On their first day in 9B, Dhruv had folded a cardboard flap from his classmate notebook into a thick, grease-stained wedge and jammed it under the short leg. The wobble ceased. From that morning onward, the bench belonged to them by right of engineering.

In the upper right-hand corner of the desk, sheltered from the teacher's line of sight by the shoulder of whoever sat in front, were two sets of initials carved into the timber with a heavy geometric compass:

*DM + SQ*

Not a heart. Hearts were for the foolish boys who wrote letters to girls from the Convent across the road and got called into the Vice Principal's office to have their ears twisted. These were block capitals, clean and deep, filled in with black fountain-pen ink until the wood grain had absorbed the pigment permanently.

Dhruv was short, broad-shouldered, and slow-moving. He had the physical economy of a boy who knows he is not fast enough to outrun anyone on the football field, so he simply positions himself where the ball is likely to bounce. He was quiet, but he was not timid; he possessed an obstinate, boulder-like calm that made other boys hesitate before trying to push him off the canteen queue.

Sameer was the opposite in every measurable way.

Sameer was tall, skinny, with wrists that stuck out of his uniform shirts three inches past the cuffs and a nose that looked as though it had been designed for a boy twice his size. He was in perpetual, vibrating motion. He tapped his ruler against the inkwell; he drummed his heels against the book rack; he threw wet paper balls at the ceiling fan to see if they would stick to the blades. He had been sent to the corridor six times in the first month of term for answering teachers with that peculiar, wide-eyed innocence that was far more insolent than outright defiance.

'Malhotra,' their class teacher, Mrs. Sen, had said during the third week of July, adjusting her horn-rimmed spectacles as she surveyed the classroom. 'You are sitting with Qureshi. Keep him quiet or you will both spend the zero period pulling weeds from the badminton court.'

Dhruv had simply nodded.

They had become inseparable through the quiet, unspoken division of labor that governs all enduring male alliances. Sameer provided the momentum, the wild ideas, and the sudden, irrational enthusiasms; Dhruv provided the ballast, the bus pass, and the half-sandwich his mother packed in silver foil.

When Sameer decided in August that they should build a periscope out of two pocket mirrors and an empty cardboard tube from an agarbatti box to observe the staff room from the staircase landing, Dhruv was the one who calculated the mirror angles so the image wouldn't come out upside down. When Sameer got caught by the discipline master smoking a dried neem twig behind the cycle shed, Dhruv walked into the master's office with a straight face and claimed they were conducting an experiment on herbal mosquito repellents for the junior science exhibition.

The master had looked at Dhruv's serious, round face, sighed, and let them off with a warning.

'You're a genius, Dhruv,' Sameer had laughed on the cycle ride home, standing on the pedals of his Atlas bicycle. 'A certified, stone-faced criminal genius.'

'Just pedal,' Dhruv had said from the luggage carrier, holding his schoolbag on his knees. 'My mother is making bread pakodas and if we're late my brother will eat four of them.'

storySections.heading: 2001 — The Daryaganj Pavement
storySections.body:
Before the engineering entrances separated us by four hundred kilometres of railway track, our Saturdays belonged to the Sunday book market on the pavements of Asaf Ali Road in Daryaganj.

It wasn't Sunday, strictly speaking—if you went on Sunday morning, the crowd from Delhi University had already picked through the burlap sacks. The real hunting happened on Saturday afternoons around four, when the wholesalers from Old Delhi unloaded the tied bundles from handcarts into the covered verandahs of the closed commercial buildings. The smell of Daryaganj in September was an indelible sensory concentrate: diesel exhaust from the Red Fort bus ring, fried bread from the kachori wallah near Delite Cinema, and millions of cubic feet of pulped, decomposing newsprint and damp textbook paper baking under forty degrees of humid heat.

Sameer walked with his hands in his pockets, his gaze raking the stacks on the tarpaulin like an industrial surveyor.

His father ran a small lathe workshop in the industrial galis behind Anand Parbat—two manual turning machines, a drill press held together with vulcanized rubber belts, and a floor permanently coated in steel shavings and dark, sulphurous coolant oil. The workshop made precision spindle pins for tractor water pumps. It was a business measured in millimeters and four-anna margins. When Sameer needed I.E. Irodov's *Problems in General Physics* and the three-volume calculus series by Piskunov, there was no question of going to Galgotia's in Connaught Place, where the clean Russian Mir Publishers editions sat behind glass cases with foil price tags.

'Watch the binding,' Sameer murmured, crouching beside a pile tied with hemp string. His fingers were quick, deft, sensitive to paper density. 'If the stitching in the spine is broken, don't touch it. The Indian reprints from Meerut use bone glue that melts by October. You lose the entire chapter on rotational dynamics right before the midterm.'

He found an original 1984 Moscow edition of Irodov—hardcover, olive-green cloth with silver embossed lettering, the pages thick, cream-toned, printed with the heavy, legible lead type of Soviet state presses. The seller, a bearded man sitting cross-legged on a folded quilt, wanted ninety rupees.

Sameer had sixty-five rupees in a folded plastic pouch tucked into the watch pocket of his jeans.

I stood beside him in my clean Bata tennis shoes, my schoolbag containing a fresh set of Faber-Castell mechanical pencils and two hundred rupees in crisp ten-rupee notes that my mother had given me before I left our government quarters in Chanakyapuri. My father was a joint director in the Ministry of Surface Transport. In our house, books were not negotiated over; they were requisitioned, purchased, and lined up alphabetically on teak shelves.

'Sameer,' I said, reaching into my pocket, 'take the thirty from me. We can get the kachoris on the way back.'

He didn't look at me, but his shoulders tightened under his cotton shirt. It was an almost imperceptible movement, the slight inward bracing of a boy who has been offered charity and is calculating how to refuse it without losing the person making the offer.

'Keep your money in your pocket, Dhruv,' he said evenly.

He turned to the bookseller. For twelve minutes, without raising his voice, without pleading, Sameer negotiated. He pointed out the faint water stain on page 142. He showed where a previous student in Kanpur had solved problem 2.14 in ballpoint ink right across the diagram. He offered sixty rupees cash and a pristine copy of a Class 11 organic chemistry guide he had carried in his own bag.

The seller grunted, took the sixty rupees, took the chemistry guide, and slapped the olive-green Irodov into Sameer's palm.

Walking back toward the Delhi Gate bus stop, Sameer held the heavy book against his ribs. His fingers traced the silver Russian lettering through the paper bag.

'You think I'm stubborn,' he said as we waited at the traffic signal. The sun was going down behind the red stone facade of the old jail, throwing long, amber shadows across the intersection.

'I think you could have just let me pay the twenty-five rupees,' I said. 'We're brothers, aren't we? What difference does twenty-five rupees make between us?'

Sameer stopped on the curb. He looked at me with his clear, dark, unblinking eyes—the eyes of a boy who understood the exact weight of steel pins and daily ledgers.

'Between you and me, no difference,' he said. 'Between your father and my father, all the difference in the world. If I start taking your money for books, Dhruv, then this desk isn't level anymore. And once a desk tilts, things start sliding off.'

I laughed then, because I was seventeen and believed that brotherhood was an invincible abstraction that floated high above economics. I bought the kachoris. He ate two, deliberately, with great appetite, making sure to pay for our bus tickets to Chanakyapuri with his remaining five-rupee note.

He kept that olive-green Irodov for twenty years. It was on the table in Pune the night we drank tea behind the wedding tent. He had used it to calculate the shear load on the cardboard wedge.

storySections.heading: 1999 — The Secretariat Bus Shelter
storySections.body:
In the July of our Class 11 year, the monsoon arrived over New Delhi with a sudden, violent crack of thunder that turned the sky over Raisina Hill the colour of bruised slate within twelve minutes.

We had just walked out of the physics tuition center in Patel Nagar. We didn't have umbrellas—seventeen-year-old boys in government colonies considered umbrellas an embarrassing concession to adult fragility—and by the time we sprinted across the traffic circle to the concrete bus shelter opposite the Central Secretariat, our cotton shirts were plastered to our ribs and water was running in grey channels through the canvas of our shoes.

My father had been transferred that week from the Ministry of Surface Transport to an obscure, windowless administrative tribunal in the Ministry of Fertilizers.

In the bureaucratic geography of Lutyens' Delhi, transfers were not logistical events; they were moral verdicts. When a joint director was moved from surface transport—where contracts were awarded and state highway commissions came calling with brass gifts at Diwali—to fertilizers, everyone in the colony understood what had happened. My father had refused to sign off on an asphalt procurement file for a national highway stretch in Haryana. He had not made a speech; he had simply written a five-line objection in the margin and sent the file back up the line. The minister's private secretary had called our landline at eight in the evening. Three days later, the blue transfer order arrived by courier.

Our house in Chanakyapuri had gone dead still.

My father sat on the balcony every evening in his cane chair, smoking three Gold Flake cigarettes in the dark, watching the headlights on Shantipath. My mother spent hours in the kitchen wiping surfaces that were already immaculate, her jaw set like concrete.

I sat in the concrete bus shelter with Sameer, shivering in the monsoon wind, watching the rain bounce two feet off the steaming asphalt.

'They're going to make us leave the Type V quarters by December,' I said, staring down at my waterlogged shoes. My voice was thin, shaking slightly with a humiliation that felt unbearable. 'My mother is already looking at flats in Rohini. Two rooms, Sameer. Shared water pump on the ground floor. My father won't even speak at dinner. He looks at me like he failed some test that everybody else passed.'

Sameer reached into his canvas bag. He pulled out a steel dabba wrapped in a piece of red checkered cloth.

Inside were two cold parathas, stuffed with spiced mashed potatoes and green chilies, cut into neat quarters by his mother's small kitchen knife.

He picked up two quarters. He handed them to me on the greaseproof paper.

'Eat,' he said.

'I'm not hungry, Sameer.'

'Eat, Dhruv,' he repeated, without raising his voice. 'Your father didn't fail anything. My father has been working the lathe in Anand Parbat for twenty-eight years. When the factory inspectors come for their monthly envelope, my father locks the gate and stands in the doorway until they show the municipal citation. The other lathe owners call him an obstinate Muslim who doesn't understand practical business. But at night, when he washes the grease off his arms with pumice soap, his skin is clean. Your father's skin is clean, Dhruv. If you have to move to Rohini, you move to Rohini. The desk stays level.'

I took the cold paratha. I ate it. The taste of cold mustard oil, roasted cumin, and pickled chili was sharp against the back of my throat.

We sat under the concrete slab while the rain beat against the road like a drum. Sameer didn't offer any more advice. He didn't tell me things would work out. He simply sat beside me on the wet concrete bench, shoulder to shoulder, his canvas bag between his knees, giving me the only thing that actually mattered: forty minutes of a boy's steady, unthreatened company while the sky fell down.

storySections.chapterTitle: Scene 3: The Summons across Twenty-Three Years (2024)
storySections.heading: Scene 3: The Summons across Twenty-Three Years (2024)
storySections.body:
The reply arrived eighty seconds after Dhruv pressed send.

His phone did not chime; it vibrated in his hand with the long, urgent buzz of an incoming voice call. The caller ID displayed the Pune number.

Dhruv's heart gave that strange, double-thump again. He sat up straight in the car seat, cleared his throat twice, and swiped the green icon.

'Hello?'

'Dhruv?'

The voice was lower, rougher around the edges, with the dry, slightly raspy texture of a man who spends half his day on dusty construction sites, but the cadence—that fast, impatient, forward-leaning rhythm—was entirely unchanged. It was the voice of a boy shouting from the front pedals of an Atlas bicycle.

'Yes,' Dhruv said. 'Sameer. It's me.'

'You bastard,' Sameer said. The word was delivered not as an insult, but with an immense, exhaled breath that sounded like ten years of held air leaving a room. 'Where the hell have you been?'

Dhruv laughed, a short, helpless bark that caught in his throat. 'Where have *I* been? You're the one who vanished into Maharashtra without leaving a forwarding address!'

'My father's department moved us three times in five years, Dhruv! We were in Nagpur, then Nashik, then Pune. I didn't even have an email address until 2004.' A pause. In the background of Sameer's phone, Dhruv could hear the loud, energetic commotion of a wedding household—women's voices calling out about flower garlands, the distant drone of a dholak, someone asking where the dry fruits had been stored. 'How did you get my number?'

'Varun Kapoor posted your wedding card in the batch group.'

'Varun? That idiot who used to wear the orange socks?' Sameer laughed, loud and sharp. 'Listen to me. The reception is on Saturday. In Pune. You are coming.'

It was not a question. It was not a polite invitation tendered to an old acquaintance with the understanding that distance and family obligations would provide a graceful excuse for declining. It was a command, issued with the absolute, unquestioning authority of Room 9.

'Sameer, it's Wednesday,' Dhruv said, leaning his forehead against the steering wheel. 'I have a job. I have two children. Pallavi's mother is visiting from Lucknow—'

'Bring Pallavi. Bring the kids. Bring her mother.'

'I can't bring a family of five to Pune on two days' notice, Sameer. Flight tickets are twelve thousand rupees each.'

'Then come alone,' Sameer said. His voice dropped into that quiet, stubborn register Dhruv remembered from eighth standard, the tone he used when he was about to do something reckless and didn't care about the consequences. 'Dhruv. You have to come. Do you remember what we said on the last day?'

The parking basement was completely silent except for the low hum of the exhaust fans.

'I remember,' Dhruv said.

'Then book the ticket,' Sameer said, and hung up.

storySections.chapterTitle: 2015 — The ICU Waiting Room in Okhla
storySections.heading: 2015 — The ICU Waiting Room in Okhla
storySections.body:
In the winter of 2015, Sameer's father suffered an ischemic stroke while unloading a crate of alloy steel bars from a Tata 407 in the Anand Parbat lane.

The metal crate had slipped from the hydraulic hoist. Master Qureshi had stepped forward instinctively to catch it—a forty-year habit of protecting material before protecting oneself—and the strain had ruptured an arterial wall in his parietal lobe. By the time they carried him to the Holy Family Hospital in Okhla, he had lost sensation across the entire right quadrant of his body and could only produce a low, rhythmic hum from the back of his throat.

I was in Singapore.

I was thirty-one, the regional head of procurement for a Swiss logistics conglomerate, staying at the Fullerton on Collyer Quay. My week was structured into fifteen-minute calendar increments: supply-chain optimization meetings, port automation demos at Jurong, dinner with regional vice-presidents at Marina Bay Sands. My phone was an iPhone 6 in a matte navy leather sleeve that buzzed every twenty seconds with alerts from Tokyo, Rotterdam, and Dubai.

Sameer sent a text on Tuesday morning at 6:14 AM: *Abba in Holy Family ICU. Stroke. Surgery scheduled 11 AM.*

I called immediately from the hotel balcony, looking down at the illuminated barges moving like water beetles across Singapore Harbor.

'Sameer? How bad is it? Have you spoken to the neurosurgeon? Listen, my cousin is a senior radiologist at Apollo in Sarita Vihar. I can get him transferred by noon in an advanced cardiac ambulance.'

'No,' Sameer's voice said. It sounded completely flat, completely exhausted, stripped of all color by forty-eight hours of fluorescent hospital lighting. 'The surgeon here is Dr. Mathew. He's very competent. The clot is in a delicate junction near the motor cortex. We can't move him.'

'How much is the deposit?' I asked. I had my laptop open on the patio table, already logging into my Citibank priority banking portal. 'I'll transfer three lakhs right now to the hospital account. Just send me the beneficiary IFSC.'

There was a long pause on the satellite connection. In the background, I could hear the public address system of Holy Family Hospital calling for a nursing supervisor in Ward 4, and the steady, wet squeak of cleaning mops on linoleum.

'Dhruv,' Sameer said quietly. 'The hospital bill is under control. The union welfare fund covered the ICU deposit, and my brother sold the secondary lathe. We don't need money.'

'Sameer, don't be an idiot! A lathe? Why are you selling machines when I'm sitting right here? Transfer takes forty seconds. Let me pay the bill.'

'I don't need your money, Dhruv,' he repeated. His tone was not angry. It was worse than angry; it was patient. 'My brother and I can handle the bill. What I needed was someone to sit with Ammi on the bench outside the theatre while they opened his skull. She doesn't speak English, Dhruv. The orderlies shout at her when she asks for warm water. She's been sitting on a steel chair since midnight holding his sandals in her lap.'

The air in my hotel room suddenly felt thin, artificial, chilled by the central HVAC to an unnatural sixteen degrees.

'I'm in Singapore, Sameer,' I whispered. 'I have the APAC steering committee at two o'clock. If I walk out now—'

'I know where you are,' he said. 'I read your LinkedIn post about the port summit yesterday. You looked very smart in your blazer.'

'Sameer—'

'Go to your committee, Dhruv. Dr. Mathew is coming out of the scrub room now. I have to sign the anesthesia indemnity.'

He disconnected.

I stood on the Fullerton balcony for ten minutes while the Singapore morning traffic hummed along the waterfront. I looked at the glass towers of the financial district, rising like silver chisels into the tropical cloud cover. I had six hundred thousand dollars in equity options, a corner apartment in Gurgaon with Italian marble skirting, and four thousand professional contacts on my phone.

And three thousand miles away, in a crowded municipal corridor smelling of carbolic acid and despair, an elderly woman in a faded cotton salwar was holding her husband's grease-stained leather sandals in her lap, and the friend who had shared my desk for four years was signing a document that gave a stranger permission to cut into his father's brain.

I sent two flower arrangements to Holy Family Hospital that afternoon—white orchids from an international delivery florist, with a card that said *Wishing Master Qureshi a speedy recovery. With prayers, Dhruv Malhotra and Family.*

The florist sent an automated confirmation email with a timestamp and a digital signature from a hospital security guard.

Sameer never mentioned the orchids. His father survived the surgery, lived for another four years with a walking stick and a speech impediment that made his voice sound like gravel being turned in a tin pan, and died peacefully in his sleep during the monsoon of 2019.

When I attended the funeral in the cemetery near Turkman Gate, Sameer embraced me at the gate. It was a proper hug—firm, brief, respectful. But when he stepped back and looked at me, there was a small, quiet perimeter drawn between our chests. It was not hostile; it was simply measurable.

We were still brothers. But we were brothers who lived on opposite sides of a glass pane.

storySections.chapterTitle: Scene 4: The Last Day of Class 9B (1998)
storySections.heading: Scene 4: The Last Day of Class 9B (1998)
storySections.body:
It was a Friday in late November when the news broke.

Sameer's father worked for the Central Public Works Department—an executive engineer who was perpetually subject to the mysterious, arbitrary transfer orders issued by the Ministry of Urban Development in New Delhi. Transfers in CPWD were like lightning strikes: they arrived without warning, gave families fourteen days to pack twelve steel trunks, and dispatched them to state capitals where they knew nobody.

Sameer had come into the classroom twenty minutes before the assembly bell. He had not taken his bag off his shoulders. He had walked straight to the last bench, pulled out the chair, and sat down with his elbows on the desk.

'We're going to Pune,' he said.

Dhruv was sharpening a pencil into the desk drawer. He stopped turning the small plastic sharpener. The pencil shavings—pale cedar smelling of resin—lay curled against his knuckles.

'When?'

'Next Friday. The packers are coming on Tuesday.'

The classroom was filling up around them. Boys were shouting across rows, comparing notes on the physics test, arguing about Sachin Tendulkar's century against Zimbabwe. The morning sun was striking the chalkboards, turning the green slate into blinding white rectangles.

Neither of them spoke for the entirety of first period.

During the short break, instead of running to the canteen for vegetable cutlets, they walked down to the far corner of the football field, near the old tamarind tree where the compound wall had crumbled into a pile of red bricks. They sat on the bricks with their knees drawn up to their chests.

'Pune is far,' Dhruv said. It was the only geographical fact he possessed about Maharashtra.

'It's twenty-six hours on the train,' Sameer said. He had looked it up in his father's railway timetable. 'The Jhelum Express.'

'Will you come back for tenth standard?'

'No. My father said we'll be there for at least four years.' Sameer picked up a pebble and threw it at the compound wall. It struck the brick with a sharp *pock* and bounced into the weeds. 'I hate it.'

'You haven't even seen it.'

'I don't need to see it. It's not here.'

They sat there until the second bell rang.

In the final period—English literature, with an elderly teacher who read Wordsworth with his eyes closed—Sameer reached into his pocket and pulled out a small, flat brass compass. It was the kind with a screw adjustment that kept the pencil arm rigid.

He didn't look at Dhruv. He leaned forward over the last bench, placed the sharp steel point against the timber next to their initials, and began scratching into the Sheesham wood.

'What are you doing?' Dhruv whispered, watching the teacher's closed eyelids. 'He'll hear you.'

'Let him hear.'

Sameer didn't stop until he had carved three deep, uneven lines:

*PROMISE*

He blew the fine wood dust off the letters. He looked at Dhruv. His eyes were wide, bright, and slightly bloodshot, as if he had been staring into a strong wind.

'My father says people forget each other in two years,' Sameer whispered. 'He said when you move cities, childhood friends disappear because everybody gets busy.'

'Your father is wrong,' Dhruv said.

'Prove it.' Sameer put his right hand flat on the desk, his palm covering the carved word and their initials. 'Promise me. When we grow up, when we get married—whoever gets married first—the other one has to be there. No excuses. No "I have work." Even if it's in America. You have to show up.'

Dhruv looked at Sameer's hand. It was a skinny hand, with ink stains on the thumb and a band-aid on the index finger from a bicycle chain slip two days earlier.

He put his own hand on top of Sameer's. His palm was broader, warmer. He pressed down until he could feel the sharp edge of the carved wood biting into the flesh beneath Sameer's fingers.

'I promise,' Dhruv said.

They didn't shake hands. They didn't sign anything. They just sat with their palms stacked on the carved wood while Wordsworth's daffodils echoed across the dusty room.

storySections.heading: The Cardboard Wedge in Pune
storySections.body:
The wedding behind the kitchen tent in Pune had thinned to a few stray relatives by two in the morning.

The caterers were hosing down the tandoor drums with municipal water, the steam rising into the cold December air smelling of charred coriander, mutton fat, and burning wood chips. In the main hall, the decorators had already begun unpinning the artificial marigold strings from the styrofoam pillars, rolling up the crimson aisle carpet in dusty five-meter lengths.

Sameer set his paper cup on the plastic folding table. He reached into the breast pocket of his charcoal wool achkan—a modest, well-tailored garment that had clearly been dry-cleaned many times—and took out a small brass tobacco tin.

He opened the tin. Inside, resting on a square of tissue paper, was a folded piece of grey cardboard.

It was roughly two inches square, folded over four times, its edges worn down to soft, fibrous rounded corners. The surface was dark with decades of industrial handling—grease from lathe spindles, graphite dust from 2B drawing pencils, and the dark, polished patina that cardboard acquires when it has been carried in pockets across thirty years.

I looked at it. My heart gave a heavy, irregular thud.

'You kept it,' I said.

'You thought I threw it away?' Sameer asked. He turned the wedge over with his thumb. 'When the school demolished the East Block in 2006 to build the computer wing, the old furniture was piled in the football field behind the boundary wall. They were selling the Sheesham desks to firewood dealers for forty rupees a hundredweight. I took an auto from Anand Parbat on a Sunday morning with a crowbar and twenty rupees for the chowkidar.'

'You went back for the desk?'

'Not the desk,' Sameer said. 'The desk was half-rotten with termite tunnels near the footrest. But the wedge was still there. Driven tight between the front-right tenon and the leg socket. The timber had shrunk around it in the heat, but the cardboard had held. It had petrified, Dhruv. Like compressed shale.'

He placed the wedge on the white plastic table between our cups.

The table had an uneven leg. It wobbled by three-quarters of an inch whenever either of us rested a forearm on the surface.

Sameer smiled—a slow, tired, beautiful smile that brought back the boy who had sat beside me through three hundred mornings of trigonometry and colonial history. He picked up the wedge, bent down, and slipped it beneath the table's front-left plastic foot.

The wobble stopped. The table sat dead flat on the gravel.

'Still works,' he said.

I looked at the cardboard under the table leg, and then I looked at Sameer. His hair was completely silver at the temples now, the skin around his eyes netted with the fine, permanent lines of a man who spends his days calculating wind shear and bearing capacities on open construction decks in the sun.

'Sameer,' I said, and my voice cracked slightly in the cold night air. 'I made a mess of things, didn't I? After college. With the money, with the jobs. I thought... I thought keeping the promise meant making enough money that neither of us would ever have to worry again.'

Sameer picked up his tea. He took a sip, looked out at the caterers packing the copper cauldrons into the back of a truck, and shook his head.

'That was your promise, Dhruv. It wasn't mine.'

'What was yours?'

'Mine was that we would never pretend,' Sameer said quietly. 'That whatever happened—whether your father became an ambassador or my father's workshop went into auction—we would look at each other across the room and see the boy with the ink on his cuff and the cardboard in his shoe. You stopped looking, Dhruv. Not because you were cruel. Because you were ashamed of how much you had compared to me. And when a man is ashamed of his own good fortune, he either becomes arrogant or he runs away. You did a little bit of both.'

The sentence fell into the silence between us without drama. It was not an accusation; it was a structural calculation.

I sat with it while the temple bells at the junction began their 3 AM chime. I felt stripped, dismantled, cleared of thirty years of corporate rhetoric.

'Is it too late?' I asked.

Sameer looked down at the table. He reached out with two fingers and tapped the white plastic surface. The table didn't move. The wedge held it firm against the stones.

'The table isn't shaking, is it?' he said.

He picked up his paper cup, tapped it against mine, and drank his cold tea under the Pune stars.

storySections.heading: Scene 5: The Journey to Pune (2024)
storySections.body:
Pallavi had looked at him on Wednesday night as though he had suffered a mild stroke.

'You are spending fourteen thousand rupees on a flight to Pune to attend the reception of a boy you haven't spoken to since Atal Bihari Vajpayee was Prime Minister?'

She was standing in the kitchen, packing school lunches for the next morning—chopping cucumbers with that brisk, rhythmic efficiency that Dhruv had admired for eight years.

'Yes,' Dhruv had said, sitting at the dining table with his laptop open to an airline booking portal.

'Why?'

He had tried to explain. He had talked about Class 9B; he had talked about the uneven bench leg; he had talked about the afternoon near the tamarind tree. But as the words left his mouth, they sounded flimsy, childish, like an adult man trying to justify an expensive purchase by citing an episode of an animated cartoon he had watched at seven.

Pallavi had stopped chopping. She had looked at his face for a long, quiet moment.

'You really feel like you owe him this, don't you?' she had said softly.

'It's not that I owe him,' Dhruv said, looking down at his hands on the table. 'It's that... if I don't go, then everything we said when we were eleven was just noise. It means childhood doesn't count for anything. It means once you turn thirty, all the promises you made before you knew how expensive the world was just get cancelled.'

Pallavi had washed her hands at the sink, dried them on the kitchen towel, and walked over to the table. She had pressed her palm against the back of his neck, right where the grey hair met his collar.

'Take the early morning flight on Saturday,' she had said. 'Come back on Sunday afternoon. And don't wear your office trousers—they make you look like an auditor.'

Now, on Saturday morning at six, Dhruv was standing in the departure terminal of Delhi Airport.

The airport was cold, bright, and smelled of expensive perfume and floor polish. He carried a small duffel bag with a dark blue kurta, a change of linen, and an envelope containing five thousand rupees in fresh, crisp five-hundred-rupee notes. He felt ridiculous and exhilarated at the same time. He had not travelled alone without an office itinerary or a family vacation schedule in eleven years.

When the plane climbed out over the grey smog of Gurgaon, turning south toward the Deccan plateau, Dhruv looked down at the tiny, rectangular grid of houses below. Somewhere down there, buried under twenty-five years of flyovers and metro pillars, was the road where he and Sameer had ridden a single Atlas bicycle, carrying a folded cardboard wedge in their pockets.

storySections.chapterTitle: Scene 6: The Reception on Senapati Bapat Road (2024)
storySections.heading: Scene 6: The Reception on Senapati Bapat Road (2024)
storySections.body:
The venue was a banquet hall called *The Grand Maratha*, set back from the flyover near Senapati Bapat Road.

It was seven in the evening. The Pune air was dry, cool, carrying the scent of roasted corn and vehicle exhaust from the highway. The entrance was flanked by two large brass lamps decorated with orange marigolds. A shehnai player sat on a raised platform near the shoe counter, his cheeks puffing rhythmically against the reed.

Dhruv walked in through the glass doors.

There were two hundred people in the hall—women in rich Paithani sarees with gold borders, men in crisp linen kurtas, young cousins gathered around the dessert counter eating kulfi from small terracotta pots. It was an elegant, warm, unpretentious gathering.

At the far end of the hall, on a stage backed with white orchids, stood the bride and groom.

Dhruv stopped near the central pillar, behind a cluster of elderly uncles in Nehru jackets.

Sameer was wearing an ivory sherwani with raw silk buttons. He had filled out across the shoulders, and his hair was cut short and neat, but the posture—that slight, forward-leaning tilt of the head, as if he were trying to hear a joke being whispered across a classroom—was unmistakable. His bride, Zoya, was a beautiful woman in an emerald green lehenga, laughing as an aunt pinned a gold brooch to her dupatta.

Dhruv stood by the pillar for ten minutes.

A sudden, paralyzing wave of self-consciousness washed over him. What was he doing here? He was an uninvited ghost from an elementary school classroom, clutching an envelope of cash, intruding on the most intimate milestone of an adult stranger's life. Sameer had dozens of friends here—college friends from Pune, colleagues from his engineering firm, cousins, in-laws. They shared a present; Dhruv shared only a piece of notched Sheesham wood.

He turned toward the exit. He actually took two steps toward the glass doors.

'Malhotra!'

The shout was loud enough to cut cleanly through the shehnai music and the chatter of two hundred guests.

Dhruv froze.

He turned around. Sameer had stepped down from the stage. He was ignoring his mother-in-law, who was holding out a plate of sweets; he was ignoring the photographer who had his camera poised for a group portrait. He was walking straight down the carpeted aisle, his long legs eating up the distance, grinning with that same infuriating, lopsided grin that had driven Mrs. Sen to distraction in 1998.

He reached Dhruv. He didn't offer a polite handshake. He grabbed Dhruv by the shoulders, pulled him in, and hugged him with a bone-cracking, ferocious strength that knocked the breath out of Dhruv's lungs.

'You made it,' Sameer whispered into his ear. His voice was shaking. 'You actually came, you idiot.'

'I had to,' Dhruv gasped against the ivory silk of Sameer's shoulder. 'You said no excuses.'

Sameer pulled back. His eyes were bright with moisture, completely unashamed in front of his two hundred wedding guests. He looked Dhruv up and down—the blue kurta, the salt-and-pepper beard, the slightly rounded stomach.

'Look at you,' Sameer said, shaking his head. 'You look like a bank manager.'

'I manage cold-chain logistics,' Dhruv corrected, smiling so hard his cheeks ached. 'It's much more boring than banking.'

'Come here,' Sameer said, taking Dhruv by the wrist and pulling him toward the stage. 'Zoya! Amma! Look who's here! This is Dhruv! The one from the last bench!'

storySections.heading: Scene 7: Paper Cups at Midnight (2024)
storySections.body:
By half past eleven, the banquet hall had emptied.

The caterers were clearing the chafing dishes, stacking white porcelain plates into plastic crates with a continuous, clattering din. The floor was littered with crushed marigold petals and discarded paper napkins. Zoya had gone upstairs to the hotel suite with her mother to change out of her heavy lehenga.

Sameer had taken off his ivory sherwani. He was sitting on two white plastic folding chairs in the alleyway behind the banquet kitchen, wearing an undershirt and his churidar trousers, his bare feet resting on the cool cement.

A tea vendor from the junction had brought them two cutting chais in brown paper cups.

The night air was cold. Overhead, between the concrete edges of the hotel building and the adjacent apartment tower, a narrow strip of Pune sky was visible—grey, washed out by city sodium lights, with only two faint stars holding their ground.

'I missed your wedding,' Sameer said quietly, blowing steam from the rim of his cup.

'You didn't know,' Dhruv said.

'I should have known. I should have looked harder.' Sameer took a sip of the sweet, ginger-heavy tea. 'After my father retired in 2008, I went back to Delhi once. For a job interview with Larsen & Toubro. I took an auto to St. Jude's.'

Dhruv turned his head. 'You did?'

'Yes. On a Saturday afternoon. The gate was open because there was some basketball coaching going on. I walked up to Room 9.'

'Was it still there?'

'The room was there. But they had renovated the whole block. Steel desks, Dhruv. Pressed plywood with blue plastic chairs bolted to the frame. Not a single wooden bench left in the entire building. The headmaster told me they had auctioned off the old furniture in 2002 to pay for computer lab wiring.'

Sameer looked down at his paper cup.

'I felt like an idiot,' he whispered. 'Standing in an empty classroom with blue plastic desks, looking for two compass scratches. I thought: it's gone. We made it up. Two eleven-year-old boys in short trousers playing at being heroes, and the school sold the evidence for twenty rupees a bench.'

Dhruv was quiet for a long moment. He reached into the pocket of his trousers and pulled out a small, folded object.

It wasn't money. It was a single piece of thick grey cardboard, four inches long, two inches wide, creased down the middle into eight tight folds until it was as dense as wood. The corners were rounded and dark with twenty-six years of handling.

He placed it on Sameer's knee.

Sameer looked down at it. He picked it up with two fingers, turning it over in the amber light from the kitchen door.

'What is this?'

'The wedge,' Dhruv said simply.

Sameer stared at him. 'The wedge?'

'The last day. Before the packers came to your house. After the final bell, while everyone was running to the gate, I went back into Room 9. I kicked the short leg of the desk, pulled out the cardboard, and put it in my geometry box. I've had it in my desk drawer ever since.'

Dhruv took a sip of his tea.

'The school can sell the timber to whoever they want,' he said. 'The wood was just furniture. We were the ones who stopped the wobble.'

Sameer sat completely motionless in the plastic chair. His large hands, scarred at the knuckles from twenty years of job sites and steel beams, held the tiny piece of grey cardboard as though it were made of spun glass.

He didn't speak for two minutes. In the kitchen behind them, a waiter dropped a metal tray, and someone shouted in Marathi about locking the ice freezer.

Then Sameer closed his fingers around the cardboard, looked at Dhruv, and smiled—that same wide, lopsided, impossible grin from Class 9B.

'You really are a certified criminal genius, Malhotra.'

'Just drink your tea,' Dhruv said, leaning his head back against the wall. 'My flight is at seven tomorrow morning, and Pallavi will kill me if I smell like biryani when I walk through the door.'
